title: Out-of-Distribution Graph Models Merging
one_liner: Merge graph models trained on different domains by learning a routing gate that decides which expert model handles which graph, without needing the original training data.
lead: You have ten graph models, each trained on graphs from a different domain. When you feed a new graph to just one model, it often fails because that model only learned patterns from its own domain. This paper solves the problem by merging all ten models into one using a routing gate: for each graph that comes in, the gate dynamically decides which expert models contribute to the answer, letting the merged model handle graphs from any domain.

problem.h2: Why one model trained on one domain fails on others
paras: A graph is a network of connected nodes: social networks, molecules, citation networks. When you train a model on graphs from one domain, it learns patterns specific to that domain. Graphs from biology have different edge densities and node types than graphs from social networks.

A beginner's first idea: just pick the best single model for the new graph. But you do not know which domain the new graph comes from, and no single model handles all domains well. The old model sees patterns it never trained on and freezes up.

callout.b: The paper merges multiple models by routing each graph to the right subset of experts.
callout.html: Instead of picking one model, ask: which combination of models learned the right patterns for this graph?

steps.text: Each pre-trained model teaches a generator to create graphs that it understands well.
Gather graphs from all generators into one dataset, mixing knowledge from all domains.
Train a gating network that learns which models handle which graph patterns best.
For each parameter in each model, multiply it by a learned mask (on or off) and blend the masked models.
The merged model now routes based on the graph it sees, combining the right experts into one answer.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the routing gate and masks
paras: The paper replaces a single static model with a dynamic routing mechanism. Each incoming graph is examined, and a gate network assigns a score to each of the pre-trained expert models. The highest-scoring experts activate; others stay quiet. Then, learned binary masks (a per-model on-off switch for each number in the model) are applied, so the active experts' weights blend together.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: domain-expert alignment scores
hidden.name: How well each model fits this graph
paras: The gate computes a single hidden number for each expert model: an alignment score. It measures how well that expert model is suited to the structure and patterns of the incoming graph. A high score means the model should vote; a low score means stay out.

The paper estimates this score by having the gate network look at the graph's structure (edge density, node features, message aggregation patterns) and output a confidence for each expert. The MoE module (mixture of experts) learns which models handle which patterns best by training on the pooled synthetic graphs.

heat.caption: Darker means higher alignment score. Highlighted experts vote on this graph.

reads.html: The gate is a small neural network that looks at the incoming graph and outputs a score between 0 and 1 for each expert model, describing how relevant that expert is.
The mixture-of-experts module's gate layer computes domain-expert alignment via learned numbers, guided by the pattern of graphs instantiated from synthetic data.

mechanism.h2: Why routing and masking fix the domain problem
paras: Each pre-trained model learned one domain's patterns deeply. When you feed it a graph from a different domain, it fails because its internal weights encoded assumptions about that domain. A simple solution would be to retrain on all domains, but you do not have the original data.

The paper's move: instead of retraining, ask each model to teach a generator. The generator learns to create synthetic graphs that the model understands. Pool all the synthetic graphs. Now train a gating network on this mixed pool. The gate learns a simple rule: look at the graph's structure and decide which models learned this pattern.

The mask is the final piece. Each model has slightly different opinions about how to process information. If two models disagree on a parameter, the mask zeros out one of them so they do not fight. This selective blend means conflicting expertise cancels out, and aligned expertise reinforces.

stages.s: Apply learned masks to each expert

math.words: For each expert model i, the gate computes an alignment score alpha_i that depends on the graph. The masked expert contribution is the model's weight theta_i multiplied by the binary mask omega_i. All masked experts are blended: final prediction equals sum over i of (alpha_i times omega_i times theta_i applied to the graph).
math.equation: y = sum_i alpha_i * omega_i * f_i(Theta_i, X)
symbols: routing score for expert i (between 0 and 1)
the learned parameters of expert model i
the prediction from expert i on graph X

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Graph arrives with 50 edges and dense node features.
Gate looks at graph: alpha_1=0.9, alpha_2=0.1, alpha_3=0.05, ..., alpha_10=0.2.
Masks learned during training: omega_1=1 (on), omega_2=0 (off), omega_3=0, ..., omega_10=1.
Expert 1 predicts class A with confidence 85; multiplied by 0.9 * 1 = 0.9 contribution.
Expert 2 predicts class B with confidence 70; multiplied by 0.1 * 0 = 0 (masked out).
Expert 10 predicts class A with confidence 80; multiplied by 0.2 * 1 = 0.2 contribution.
Final blend: (0.9 * 85 + 0.2 * 80) / (0.9 + 0.2) = 83, leaning toward class A. Two aligned experts vote; the disagreeing one stays silent.

math.note: The gate is learned to route by graph structure, not domain label, so it works on any new graph.

items.b: Generator does not learn the model's patterns.
items.html: If the synthetic graph generator only copies easy patterns and misses the nuanced way the expert model processes information, the merged model will inherit incomplete knowledge. The paper solves this by having each generator minimize agreement with its expert, forcing it to learn what the expert cares about.

If the training graphs do not fairly represent all domains, the gate may overfit to surface features and route poorly on new graphs from an under-represented domain, because it learned a shortcut that worked on the imbalanced training set but fails on new patterns.

If the pre-trained models were trained very differently (e.g., one uses graph message-passing, one uses simple node averaging), the masks may have to zero out so many numbers that the merged model becomes weak. The paper gently steers masks away from extreme sparsity with a penalty term.
If the gate is trained to score each graph individually, and the masks are steered to keep most numbers active, the method blends diverse expertise smoothly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take three pre-trained graph models, each trained on a different domain (e.g., citation networks, social graphs, molecular structures). Synthesize new graphs from each model's generator. Pool them into one training set. Train a gating network and masks on this mixed pool. Then test: feed the merged model a new graph from each of the three domains plus a domain you did not see during training. The merged model should outperform each individual model on every domain, because the gate dynamically routes to the models that learned that domain's patterns, avoiding the trap of locking into one static choice.
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy = (number of correct predictions on new graphs) / (total number of new graphs), separately for each domain. Compare merged model accuracy to best individual model accuracy per domain.
demo.closing: The merged model should score higher on all four domains (three seen, one unseen) than any single pre-trained model, proving that routing to dynamic expert combinations generalizes better than any static choice, because the gate adjusts which experts vote based on the incoming graph, whereas a single model always uses the same locked-in weights.
